oneLiner: The database incumbent that bet the balance sheet on AI infrastructure: a $638B backlog and 93% OCI growth set against negative $23.7B free cash flow, $100B-plus of debt, and a stock still down more than half from its 2025 high.
thesis: The backlog is real and enormous. RPO ended fiscal 2026 (May 2026, reported Jun 10, 2026) at $638B, up 363% YoY and up $85B sequentially, with $67B of new AI infrastructure contracts signed in Q4 alone.

OCI is growing at a pace no other hyperscaler matches. OCI revenue rose 93% YoY to $5.8B in Q4 FY26, and management guided Q1 FY27 cloud revenue growth of 58-64% and FY27 total revenue of roughly $90B, up 34% in constant currency.

The bet is debt-funded, which is the whole controversy. FY26 capex was $55.7B (versus $21.2B in FY25), free cash flow was negative $23.7B, and Oracle raised $43B of debt plus $5B of equity, with roughly $40B more financing planned against a $70B FY27 net capex outlay.

Customer concentration cuts both ways. Roughly $300B of the backlog is attributed by press reports to OpenAI/Stargate commitments (not company-confirmed): transformational if OpenAI keeps paying, existential capex if it cannot.

The de-rating has already happened. From a $345.68 52-week high (Sept 2025) the stock fell as low as $114.50 before recovering to about $153 by Aug 12, 2026, leaving it near 19x the $8.05 FY27 EPS guide, a discount to MSFT and GOOGL despite far faster contracted growth.

latestProse: Oracle's fiscal Q4 FY26 (reported Jun 10, 2026) beat on both lines, with $19.18B of revenue and $2.03 of non-GAAP EPS, but the income statement is no longer the story. RPO exploded to $638B, up $85B sequentially, as another $67B of AI infrastructure contracts signed, while OCI grew 93% to $5.8B. Underneath, the strain shows: FY26 capex of $55.7B swamped roughly $32B of operating cash flow, leaving free cash flow at negative $23.7B, funded by $43B of new debt and $5B of equity. Q4 margins held (non-GAAP operating income up 22%), but management conceded FY27 gross margin steps down on data-center ramp timing and mix. The disclosure that matters most: $75B of the RPO is prepaid or customer-supplied hardware, a candid admission of how much backlog quality depends on counterparties' own funding.
guidanceProse: For FY27 Oracle guided total revenue up 34% in constant currency to roughly $90B, Q1 FY27 cloud revenue growth of 58-64%, and non-GAAP EPS of $8.05, implying continued margin compression as low-margin AI infrastructure becomes a bigger slice of the mix. The capex guide is the number that matters: a $70B net cash outlay for FY27, with roughly $40B of additional financing planned on top of a debt stack already above $100B. Management frames the margin step-down as temporary, expecting infrastructure margins to improve as data centers reach full contractual revenue contribution. Any slip in that conversion timeline flows straight into the leverage story.

guide.label: FY27 outlook
guide.sub: non-GAAP EPS $8.05; $70B net capex outlay with ~$40B new financing; gross margin steps down on AI infrastructure mix

segments: Cloud infrastructure (OCI): $5.8B in Q4 FY26, up 93% YoY; the growth engine, but capital-hungry and margin-dilutive during the buildout
Cloud applications (Fusion, NetSuite): $4.1B in Q4 FY26, up 10% YoY; the steady, high-margin SaaS base
Legacy license, support, hardware, and services: slow-growing, but still the cash cow funding the transition
competitive: MSFT/Azure: larger and self-funded from roughly $70B of annual free cash flow; Oracle is the only hyperscaler-scale builder financing capex primarily with debt
AMZN/AWS: the scale leader that Oracle undercuts on large GPU-cluster pricing and network interconnect; AWS grows a fraction as fast as OCI's 93%, but off a vastly larger base
GOOGL/GCP: the closest analog in using AI demand to gain infrastructure share, but with a fortress balance sheet behind it
SAP: the applications rival relevant to Fusion and NetSuite, and entirely absent from the AI infrastructure land grab
Neoclouds (CoreWeave and peers): compete for the same AI training contracts with even more aggressive debt structures, and set the marginal price of GPU capacity
moat: The database franchise and the enterprise install base are a genuine moat with decades of switching costs, and they fund everything else. OCI's edge, price-performance on large GPU clusters and a willingness to build to a single customer's specification, is an execution advantage rather than a structural one; commodity GPUs plus debt is a replicable formula. The $638B backlog is contractual protection, but its value is only as good as the counterparties behind it.
risks: OpenAI concentration: reportedly around $300B of RPO depends on one unprofitable counterparty's ability to keep raising capital
Debt spiral: total debt above $100B, $43B raised in FY26 and roughly $40B more planned for FY27; a credit-market shock or ratings action raises the cost of the entire strategy
Negative free cash flow (negative $23.7B in FY26) persists through at least FY27 on management's own capex guide, removing the buyback cushion that historically supported the multiple
Margin mix: AI infrastructure carries structurally lower gross margins than license and support; FY27 gross margin steps down, and 'temporary' could prove permanent if GPU rental pricing deflates

Asset obsolescence: GPUs depreciate fast, and data centers built for today's chips risk aging out before contracts fully monetize (the 'yesterday's data centers with tomorrow's debt' critique, CNBC, Mar 9, 2026)
TikTok entanglement: the 15% stake in the TikTok USDS joint venture (valued near $2B in a Mar 2026 filing) adds geopolitical and operational exposure disproportionate to its financial size
catalysts: Fiscal Q1 FY27 earnings (expected Sept 2026): first read on the 58-64% cloud growth guide and the pace of RPO-to-revenue conversion
Oracle AI World conference (expected Oct 2026, date unverified): historically the venue for new mega-contract announcements
FY27 debt issuance (roughly $40B of financing planned): pricing and rating-agency reaction will mark the market's tolerance for the strategy
OpenAI/Stargate funding rounds and data-center completions through 2026-27: each one de-risks or re-risks a large share of the backlog
TikTok USDS joint venture developments (Oracle holds 15% alongside Silver Lake and MGX; ByteDance retains 19.9%)
pricedIn: At about $153 (Aug 12, 2026 close), ORCL trades near 19x the $8.05 FY27 EPS guide: cheaper than MSFT, GOOGL, and its own recent history, for a company guiding 34% revenue growth. The market has priced in substantial doubt. The stock remains down roughly 56% from its September 2025 high of $345.68, while consensus (average target near $247, Buy rating) implies analysts believe far more of the backlog than the tape does. Priced in: continued negative free cash flow, FY27 margin compression, and meaningful OpenAI counterparty risk. Not priced in: either a clean RPO-to-revenue conversion or an OpenAI funding failure that strands the capex. This is a binary being quoted as a coin flip with a debt overhang.

scenarios.bear: OpenAI's funding stumbles in 2027 and Stargate buildouts slow; portions of RPO are re-termed or cancelled while the $70B FY27 capex is already committed. Gross margins keep sliding as GPU rental pricing deflates, EPS undershoots the $8.05 guide, and rating agencies act on a debt stack heading toward $140B. With no free-cash-flow cushion, the equity re-rates on stressed earnings: 12-13x on roughly $7 of EPS points back toward the $90-110 range, below the 52-week low.
scenarios.base: The backlog converts on schedule but unevenly: FY27 revenue lands near $90B with EPS around $8, free cash flow stays negative through FY27 and approaches breakeven in FY28 as early data centers reach full contractual contribution. Debt peaks without a downgrade spiral. The multiple recovers modestly to 21-23x forward as conversion evidence accumulates, supporting a $170-185 stock over 12 months, earned quarter by quarter against the leverage clock.
scenarios.bull: AI training demand stays supply-constrained, OpenAI keeps raising capital, and Oracle signs further non-OpenAI mega-deals that dilute concentration risk. Cloud revenue compounds 40%-plus into FY28, infrastructure margins inflect upward on utilization, and free cash flow turns positive earlier than feared. EPS runs toward $10-11 by FY28 and the market re-pays a mid-20s multiple on a de-risked backlog: a $250-plus stock, back toward the consensus target near $247.

valPresets.note: forward-earnings basis: FCF is deeply negative during the OCI/Stargate buildout; also flag the debt-funded nature of the capex
